🎃 Boo! Can you believe it's almost Halloween?

We've got some treats for you today, including a look at advancements in EV charging.
Plus, find out how Axios Publisher Nicholas Johnston spends his time in a Cybercab.

1,914 words, a 7-minute read.

1 big thing: Why EVs aren't powering the grid yet
Illustration: Megan Robinson/Axios

Electric cars have been touted for years as a secret weapon against the growing crunch on America's electricity grid. So why aren't we using them?

Why it matters: As electricity demand surges from AI data centers and manufacturing, millions of parked EVs could help utilities manage power shortages, lower costs and keep the lights on.

The big picture: The theory is simple enough: EV batteries can store electricity from the grid when it's plentiful and supply it when demand peaks.

But expensive equipment, complicated utility regulations and consumer skepticism have kept vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology from catching on.

Driving the news: Ford says its new Fathom electric pickup, arriving in 2027, could help break the logjam by slashing the cost of two-way charging.

The truck, starting below $30,000, has a built-in inverter that converts the battery's electricity into power homes can use, eliminating a costly piece of external equipment.
Ford estimates its new home charging and backup-power hardware will cost roughly $2,100, compared with about $5,200 for its existing system. Final prices haven't been announced.
Simpler installation could cut costs further.

Follow the money: EV owners could save money — or even get paid — for sharing their batteries.

They could charge their trucks when electricity is cheap, then use the stored energy to power their homes when rates are high, saving an estimated $30 to $60 per month, Ford estimates.
They can also earn rewards from utilities for charging or sending power to the grid at the right times.

California utility PG&E says drivers in its pilot program could potentially earn $600 per season by supplying electricity during periods of high demand, though actual payments vary.

To ease fears of draining their car's battery, consumers could set limits on how much power utilities could draw.

Reality check: Despite years of promises, V2G adoption remains tiny.

PG&E, a pioneer in the technology, says fewer than 70 customers have enrolled in its V2G pilot program, despite 19 eligible EV models.

Between the lines: PG&E's Kristin Landry, who leads the program, says there are three obstacles — availability, affordability and accessibility.

Cheaper equipment and more compatible vehicles could address the first two.
But utilities still face a complicated process of integrating different vehicle systems into the grid.
"Each of these bidirectional charging products is wired differently," Landry tells Axios, which adds complexity in a fragmented industry.

There's also a chicken-and-egg problem: Utilities need enough participating EVs to make grid programs worthwhile, while drivers need easy enrollment and financial incentives to justify the investment.

PG&E offers up to $4,000 in equipment incentives, yet cumbersome paperwork — like obtaining an electrician's affidavit — has discouraged some customers from enrolling, Landry acknowledges.
Ford says it's working with five major utilities to simplify the approval process for customers who want to send electricity back to the grid.

The bottom line: Ford may be making bidirectional power affordable. Making it commonplace will take a lot more than cheaper technology.

2. ⚡️ EV charging tease
I entertained myself playing Solitaire on the Lyriq's enormous touchscreen while charging at a Tesla Supercharger. Photo: Bill Rapai for Axios

Electric vehicle charging is getting tantalizingly close to effortless, as I discovered on a recent road trip through the Pacific Northwest.

But every time I thought we'd finally arrived at charging nirvana, some little annoyance reminded me that we're not quite there yet.

Why it matters: Public charging has long been one of the biggest obstacles to EV adoption. Now, automakers are finally eliminating some of the hassles that keep many drivers tethered to gasoline.

🌲 What we did: My husband and I spent two weeks exploring the Oregon Coast and Washington's Olympic Peninsula in a 2026 Cadillac Lyriq on loan from General Motors' press fleet.

I worried about finding fast-chargers in remote areas, especially within the sprawling Olympic National Park. That wasn't really an issue, though, thanks to the Lyriq's 300-plus mile driving range.
And I was eager to test GM's new Energy Pass, which streamlines the charging experience — a major pain point for EV drivers — by bringing multiple charging networks into one app, something other carmakers do, too.

🔍 How it works: You only have to enroll once in Energy Pass and add a payment method.

Then you can find, activate and pay for charging at participating networks, including Tesla, Electrify America, IONNA and Chargepoint. EVGo is coming soon.
At some chargers, you just click a button on GM's app to start the session.
It's even easier at networks that support Plug & Charge: You plug in the cable and walk away. The car and charger recognize each other, and payment happens automatically.

Zoom out: Tesla has long set the standard for such a seamless experience at its Supercharger network.

Now the rest of the industry is catching up by adopting Tesla's North American Charging Standard (NACS), and gaining access to its network.
Even cars like the 2026 Lyriq, which use the older CCS standard, can charge at many Superchargers with an adapter. (The 2027 Lyriq will have a NACS port to make it even easier.)

Yes, but: Charging speeds in the Lyriq were sometimes disappointing.

😩 There were other frustrations, too. Tesla's notoriously short Supercharger cables couldn't reach the Lyriq's front-left charging port unless we parked awkwardly, taking up two spaces.
And unlike gas stations, most charging sites offered no protection from the elements. Only one stop — at an IONNA station — had a lighted canopy overhead.

What they're saying: GM officials said we likely didn't sufficiently precondition the car's battery.

If you plug in an EV when the battery is cold, it will take longer to charge. Using the car's built-in navigation system will automatically prepare the battery ahead of the next charging stop, they said.

The bottom line: EV charging has improved enormously since my first EV road trip in 2023.

I've glimpsed nirvana. Now I just want to experience it at every stop.

3. Honda: North America should unite against China
Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios

Honda is urging the U.S., Canada and Mexico to coordinate policies to keep Chinese automakers from gaining a foothold in the American market — even as it acknowledges their arrival is ultimately inevitable.

Why it matters: Chinese automakers are expanding rapidly around the world with inexpensive, technologically sophisticated vehicles, putting pressure on established carmakers to move faster and slash costs.

"We're not going to be able to keep them out forever," Jennifer Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs at American Honda, told reporters during a roundtable discussion Tuesday.
The challenge, she said, is using that time to become more competitive before Chinese automakers arrive.

Driving the news: Honda is pressing Washington to use upcoming negotiations over the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade agreement (USMCA) to coordinate restrictions on Chinese vehicles and investment across North America.

In Canada, Honda has objected to a new import quota allowing up to 49,000 Chinese vehicles annually and is urging officials not to expand it or to encourage Chinese automotive investment in the country.
In Mexico, where Chinese brands already have a significant presence, Honda is delivering a similar message.

Between the lines: Honda has large factories in both countries that supply U.S. dealerships.

Thomas said USMCA negotiations could strengthen rules of origin to prevent Chinese vehicles or components from entering the U.S. through its neighbors.

What they're saying: "The U.S. can't do it alone," Thomas said. "It's going to take working with our neighbors to the north and south, working with allies like Japan in order to combat this threat."

The intrigue: Honda's position is striking for a Japanese automaker that helped transform the American auto industry through foreign competition decades ago.

"It's not lost on me that Honda, a company that has thrived through free trade and foreign direct investment here in this country, is advocating so aggressively to keep another international OEM out of this market," Thomas acknowledged.
She argued that Chinese automakers benefit from government support that makes fair competition difficult.

Meanwhile, Honda is racing to become more competitive through an internal initiative called "Triple Half," aimed at cutting vehicle development time, costs and workload by 50% compared with 2025 levels over the next several years.

The company is also pushing for passage of the bipartisan Connected Vehicles Security Act, which would strengthen existing restrictions on Chinese vehicle technology.

Reality check: Thomas believes Chinese automakers will eventually break through because American consumers will demand their affordable, high-tech vehicles.

As Americans encounter Chinese cars in Canada and Mexico, she said, they'll increasingly wonder why they can't buy them at home.
"I think it comes from the bottom up, and that is ultimately hard to stop, hard to contain," she said.

Share this

4. Drive-thru
Illustration: Annelise Capossela/Axios

🇨🇳 Volkswagen plans to export China-developed technology to overseas markets as it searches for ways to improve its global competitiveness. The once-unthinkable strategic shift is similar to moves Stellantis made earlier this year in response to Chinese automakers' explosive growth. (Reuters)

👆 What they're saying: "VW is turning to China and Xpeng to solve its software challenges after a series of painful billion-dollar false starts trying to get the job done with German engineers," says Michael Dunne, CEO of Dunne Insights and author of the upcoming book, "Car Wars: How China Seized the Auto Industry and How America Can Win It Back."

📈 GM is moving its stock listing from the New York Stock Exchange to Nasdaq, reflecting its growing emphasis on AI, autonomy and software-defined vehicles. GM has long argued that it deserves a tech-company valuation. (Axios)

🌎 Rivian acquired Third Dimension, a U.K.-based startup that creates 3D worlds for gaming, to help it accelerate self-driving technology. (TechCrunch)

⛽️ GM plans to introduce hybrid versions of its popular three-row SUVs, the Chevrolet Traverse, Buick Enclave and GMC Acadia, a switch after heavily investing in electric vehicles, Reuters scooped.

5. 🚖 What's driving Nick
You can watch "The Axios Show" on YouTube while riding in Tesla's driverless Cybercab. Image: Nicholas Johnston/Axios

I assigned my boss, Axios Publisher Nicholas Johnston, a self-proclaimed AV aficionado, to file a dispatch from a Tesla Cybercab while he was visiting Austin recently.

Why it matters: I personally haven't gotten to Texas yet for a ride in the gull-winged autonomous taxi.

And it's fun to make your boss do work!

Nick's big takeaway: The Cybercab is "a great robot-driven ride and a very cool car."

Plus, he got to watch his favorite show on YouTube. 👆

Zoom in: Nick used Cybercabs to get to and from his hotel in The Domain to Axios events near downtown.

The rides seemed a bit cheaper than comparable Ubers, he said, and wait times were short after downloading the app.
It's a confident driver, changing lanes to pass slower cars and zipping through yellow-light intersections like a human, he said.
Like other self-driving cars, it can struggle sometimes at crowded intersections when it's navigating stop signs and pedestrians.
"The ride was a lot smoother than the jostling I got in a Lyft ride from the airport," he wrote. "It also picked me up where I wanted and dropped me off where I wanted; no walking to specific spots."

Yes, but: The absence of a steering wheel or mirrors can be disorienting when you want to look behind the car and reflexively glance to the side (though you can turn on cameras).

The Cybercab didn't have highway access, either, which made his trips 15 to 20 minutes longer, he estimates.

1 juvenile thing: You can tip the robot driver 69 cents or $4.20 after the ride.

 Can a Portable Power Station Charge an Electric Vehicle in an Emergency?
 Stranded with 0% battery in your EV? Can a portable power station actually give you enough juice to reach the next charging station? Here is what you need to know.
 Last updated: July 20, 2026 
 6 min read 
 Admin 
 Direct answer: Stranded with 0% battery in your EV? Can a portable power station actually give you enough juice to reach the next charging station? Here is what you need to know.
 It's the ultimate nightmare for any EV owner: you're miles from the nearest charging station, and the battery percentage drops to 0%. Your car comes to a halt.
 Can a portable power station save you from calling a tow truck? The short answer is yes , but there are some major caveats.
 The Math Behind EV Charging
 Electric vehicle batteries are massive. A Tesla Model Y Long Range has an roughly 75kWh (75,000Wh) battery. 
 A standard large portable power station, like the EcoFlow DELTA 2, has a 1,024Wh capacity. 
 This means that totally draining a 1,024Wh power station will only charge a Tesla Model Y by about 1.3%. However, in an EV, 1.3% battery can get you roughly 3 to 4 miles of range . 
 If you are just a few miles short of a Supercharger, that portable power station is a lifesaver.
 What Do You Need to Make it Work?
 You cannot just plug any power bank into an EV. You need to meet two specific requirements:
 Pure Sine Wave Inverter: EVs are incredibly sensitive to electrical current. You must use a power station with a Pure Sine Wave inverter (which most premium models have). Modified sine wave inverters will be rejected by the car.
 Adequate Wattage: The power station must be able to output at least 1,500W to 1,800W continuously to satisfy the car's standard Level 1 mobile charging cable.
 Grounding Adapter (Crucial): Because power stations use a floating ground, a Tesla (and most EVs) will reject the charge, thinking there is a dangerous electrical fault. You must purchase a Neutral-Ground Bonding Plug and plug it into one of the power station's AC outlets to trick the car into accepting the charge.
 Best Power Stations for an EV Rescue
 If you are carrying a power station specifically for EV rescues, you need capacity. We recommend looking at models in the 2,000Wh+ range:
 EcoFlow DELTA Pro (3,600Wh): Could provide 10-12 miles of emergency range.
 Bluetti AC200MAX (2,048Wh): Could provide 5-8 miles of emergency range.
 Anker SOLIX F2000 (2,048Wh): Could provide 5-8 miles of emergency range.
 Conclusion
 While you certainly shouldn't rely on a portable power station to regularly top up your EV, keeping a large power station in the boot equipped with a neutral-ground bonding plug provides incredible peace of mind for long road trips through charging deserts.

 Electric vehicles are becoming the norm on roads across Canada and beyond. Yet one concern persists among both new and experienced EV drivers: What happens if the battery runs out far from a charging station? This is where portable power solutions step in. With advancements in portable power station technology, EV owners now have backup charging options that were unthinkable several years ago.
 This article explores exactly what an emergency EV recharge from a power station can achieve, how it works, what limitations exist, and which devices offer the best reliability for real-world roadside situations.

 Can a Portable Power Station Charge an EV in an Emergency? 
 The short answer: Yes — but not to full capacity. A high-output  best power station  can provide enough energy to get your EV to the nearest public charger. While it won’t replace a Level 2 home charger or DC fast charging station, it can deliver a lifesaving “boost” when your battery drops to zero.
 Before diving into numbers, let’s look at how this works.
 How EV Emergency Charging Works 
 A portable power station equipped with AC output and a stable  power inverter solar  system can supply electricity to your EV’s portable Level 1 charger. This is typically a 120V trickle charger that comes with most EVs.
 In emergency conditions, you would:
 Connect the EV’s Level 1 charger to the portable power station.
 Allow the system to deliver slow, steady power to the EV battery.
 Gain enough miles or kilometers to reach the closest charging point.
 This method is slow, but effective when you need a short-range “rescue”.
 What Level of Charge Can You Expect? 
 This depends on:
 Battery capacity of the portable generators 
 EV energy consumption per km or mile
 Ambient temperature
 Charging efficiency (typically ~85%)
 As a rule of thumb:
 A high-capacity portable power station (1,500–2,400Wh) provides 5–12 km (3–8 miles) of emergency driving range.
 Using an expansion battery can increase that significantly.
 It’s not meant for daily EV charging — only critical situations.
 Limitations of EV Emergency Charging with Portable Power Stations 
 Although emergency charging is possible and practical, it’s important to understand what a power station cannot do.
 It C annot Replace Home or Public Charging 
 A portable power station lacks the voltage, continuous wattage, and cooling systems required for Level 2 or fast charging. It only supports Level 1 trickle charging.
 Charging Speed Is Slow 
 Typical power output for Level 1 EV chargers is:
 1,300W–1,500W
 8–12 hours for a meaningful charge (from a wall outlet)
 From a portable power station, you get:
 A short emergency buffer
 Not a travel-ready recharge
 Energy Losses Reduce Efficiency 
 Charging involves inverter conversion losses, meaning you don’t get 100% of the stored watt-hours into the car battery. Expect around 75–85% efficiency.
 When Does Emergency EV Charging Make Sense? 
 Emergency EV charging isn’t something most drivers will use often — but in the right situations, it can be a lifesaver.
 Perfect Scenarios for Portable EV Rescue Power 
 You’ll benefit most if you:
 Drive long rural routes with few charging stations
 Camp off-grid or visit festivals where charging access is limited
 Live in cold climates where EV range decreases
 Share one household charger and occasionally run low unexpectedly
 Want a safety backup for winter travel
 In these cases, keeping a high-capacity portable power station in your trunk is excellent insurance.

 When selecting a device for EV backup charging, capacity, output stability, and lifespan are key.

 Can a Portable Power Station Top Up an Electric Vehicle?
 16/09/2026 | Anker 
 Blog Center 
 All 
 Yes, but only as an emergency stopgap, and only by a small amount. A portable power station can add a modest trickle of range to an electric vehicle through its slow charger, but it holds a fraction of what an EV's battery needs, so a full charge is out of the question. The honest framing is emergency-only: enough to reach a charge point or edge a stranded car to safety. Think of it as a jerry can, not a filling station, and plan accordingly.

 Key Takeaways
 A portable power station can only add a small, slow top-up to an electric vehicle.
 The energy stored is a fraction of a car battery's needs, so a full charge is unrealistic.
 This is an emergency-only tactic to reach a charge point, not a regular charging method.
 Only a high-capacity portable power station is worth considering for the task.
 Why EV Charging Is a Different Scale of Energy
 The gap in scale is the whole story. An electric vehicle's battery stores an enormous amount of energy compared with even a large portable power station, so pouring one into the other is like topping up a swimming pool with a watering can. You can make a difference, but it is a small one measured in a handful of miles rather than a usable day of driving. Once you grasp that scale, the role of a portable power station becomes clear: emergency assistance, not everyday charging.
 What a Realistic Top-Up Looks Like
 In practice, a high-capacity portable power station can deliver enough to move a stranded electric vehicle a short distance or reach the nearest charge point. The transfer happens through the car's slow, trickle charger, so it is measured in hours and adds only a modest buffer of range. That is genuinely useful in a bind — it can be the difference between a tow and a short crawl to a charger — but it is not a substitute for proper infrastructure. Set your expectations low and you will be glad to have it.
 Why a Full Charge Is Out of Reach
 A full charge demands far more energy than any portable power station stores, and the slow-charge rate means the transfer is inefficient and gradual. Even a high-capacity unit would empty itself entirely for a small fraction of the car's range. Anker SOLIX portable power stations are superb at powering appliances, tools and electronics, but no battery of their size is built to refill an electric vehicle. Treat EV top-up as a niche, emergency capability rather than a headline feature.

 What to Look For in a Portable Power Station for EV Top-Up
 If you want even a chance of topping up an electric vehicle, only a high-capacity unit makes sense, and you will need the correct charging lead and an output that matches your car's slow-charging requirements. A battery management system and LiFePO4 chemistry keep the unit stable and safe during a long, steady discharge. Anker SOLIX portable power stations offer the capacity, clean output and protection that a careful emergency top-up demands — but remember that even the best unit tops up, it does not refuel.
 Conclusion
 A portable power station can top up an electric vehicle in an emergency, but only by a small, slow amount and only with a high-capacity unit. It is a safety net to reach a charge point, not a replacement for one. Anker SOLIX portable power stations give you a dependable reserve of clean power that can edge a stranded car to safety, making them a useful part of your contingency kit — just keep the jerry-can mindset, and you will never be disappointed.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can a portable power station charge an electric car?
 Only in emergencies, and only a small amount. A high-capacity portable power station can deliver a slow trickle that adds a few miles of range, enough to reach a charge point. A full charge is out of reach because the unit stores a fraction of a car battery's energy.
 How much range can a power station add to an EV?
 Only a small buffer of range, measured in a handful of miles at best. The transfer runs through the car's slow trickle charger, so it is gradual and limited. A high-capacity portable power station helps in a bind, but it is no substitute for a proper charger.
 What size power station do I need for EV charging?
 A high-capacity portable power station is the realistic minimum, and even that only tops up an electric vehicle in an emergency. Compact and mid-range units hold too little energy to matter. You will also need the correct charging lead for your car.
 Is topping up an EV with a power station efficient?
 Not especially. The slow-charge transfer is gradual and loses some energy along the way, and the unit holds only a fraction of what an electric vehicle needs. It is a sensible emergency measure for a few miles of range, but it is not an efficient charging method.
 Why can't a power station fully charge an EV?
 Because the energy scales are wildly different. An electric vehicle's battery stores far more than even a large portable power station, and the slow-charge rate caps how quickly it can transfer. A unit that refills a phone and runs a fridge cannot refuel a car.
 Is a portable power station a good EV emergency backup?
 Yes, as a last resort. It can edge a stranded electric vehicle to a charge point and needs no fuel, making it clean and quiet. Just treat it as a safety net for a few miles of range, not a reliable way to extend every journey.

 EV Emergency Charging from a Power Station: What's Possible?
 19/01/2026 | Anker 
 Centre de blogs

 Electric vehicles are becoming the norm on roads across Canada and beyond. Yet one concern persists among both new and experienced EV drivers: What happens if the battery runs out far from a charging station? This is where portable power solutions step in. With advancements in portable power station technology, EV owners now have backup charging options that were unthinkable several years ago.
 This article explores exactly what an emergency EV recharge from a power station can achieve, how it works, what limitations exist, and which devices offer the best reliability for real-world roadside situations.
 Can a Portable Power Station Charge an EV in an Emergency?

 Final Thoughts — What’s Possible with EV Emergency Charging? 
 Can a Portable Power Station Charge an EV in an Emergency? 
 The short answer: Yes — but not to full capacity. A high-output  best power station  can provide enough energy to get your EV to the nearest public charger. While it won’t replace a Level 2 home charger or DC fast charging station, it can deliver a lifesaving “boost” when your battery drops to zero.
 Before diving into numbers, let’s look at how this works.
 How EV Emergency Charging Works 
 A portable power station equipped with AC output and a stable  power inverter solar  system can supply electricity to your EV’s portable Level 1 charger. This is typically a 120V trickle charger that comes with most EVs.
 In emergency conditions, you would:
 Connect the EV’s Level 1 charger to the portable power station.
 Allow the system to deliver slow, steady power to the EV battery.
 Gain enough miles or kilometers to reach the closest charging point.
 This method is slow, but effective when you need a short-range “rescue”.
 What Level of Charge Can You Expect? 
 This depends on:
 Battery capacity of the portable generators 
 EV energy consumption per km or mile
 Ambient temperature
 Charging efficiency (typically ~85%)
 As a rule of thumb:
 A high-capacity portable power station (1,500–2,400Wh) provides 5–12 km (3–8 miles) of emergency driving range.
 Using an expansion battery can increase that significantly.
 It’s not meant for daily EV charging — only critical situations.
 Limitations of EV Emergency Charging with Portable Power Stations 
 Although emergency charging is possible and practical, it’s important to understand what a power station cannot do.
 It C annot Replace Home or Public Charging 
 A portable power station lacks the voltage, continuous wattage, and cooling systems required for Level 2 or fast charging. It only supports Level 1 trickle charging.
 Charging Speed Is Slow 
 Typical power output for Level 1 EV chargers is:
 1,300W–1,500W
 8–12 hours for a meaningful charge (from a wall outlet)
 From a portable power station, you get:
 A short emergency buffer
 Not a travel-ready recharge
 Energy Losses Reduce Efficiency 
 Charging involves inverter conversion losses, meaning you don’t get 100% of the stored watt-hours into the car battery. Expect around 75–85% efficiency.
 When Does Emergency EV Charging Make Sense? 
 Emergency EV charging isn’t something most drivers will use often — but in the right situations, it can be a lifesaver.
 Perfect Scenarios for Portable EV Rescue Power 
 You’ll benefit most if you:
 Drive long rural routes with few charging stations
 Camp off-grid or visit festivals where charging access is limited
 Live in cold climates where EV range decreases
 Share one household charger and occasionally run low unexpectedly
 Want a safety backup for winter travel
 In these cases, keeping a high-capacity portable power station in your trunk is excellent insurance.

 When selecting a device for EV backup charging, capacity, output stability, and lifespan are key.
 Among the most reliable options on the market, the Anker SOLIX lineup stands out.
 Why Anker SOLIX Portable Power Stations Are Ideal

Can a Portable Power Station Charge an EV? Emergency Top-Up Guide — Descent Analysis 
 Can a Portable Power Station Charge an EV? Emergency Top-Up Guide
 Volume I  ·  May 2026  ·  971 words
A recurring question in portable power station forums: can a power station
charge an electric vehicle in an emergency? The short answer is yes — but the
energy math is unforgiving, and the practical use case is narrower than most
buyers expect. This article quantifies what a portable power station can and
cannot do for EV emergency top-up.
 The Energy Math
An electric vehicle battery stores 40–100 kWh. A portable power station
stores 0.3–2 kWh — two to three orders of magnitude less. The question is
not whether a power station can fully charge an EV (it cannot, by a factor of
40–300) but whether it can provide enough energy to reach the nearest
functional charger.
EV efficiency at moderate speeds (40–60 km/h) ranges from 5–8 km per
kWh for most passenger vehicles. A 768 Wh power station — one of the
larger portable units — holds 0.768 kWh. Accounting for 85% charging
efficiency (AC inverter losses in the power station + AC-DC conversion losses
in the EV's onboard charger), usable energy delivered to the battery is
approximately 0.65 kWh:
0.65 kWh × 6 km/kWh ≈ 3.9 km (2.4 miles) of range
A EcoFlow River 2 Pro 
(768 Wh) adds approximately 4 km of range to a typical EV. A
 Jackery Explorer 300 Plus 
(288 Wh) adds approximately 1.5 km. A large unit like the
 Bluetti AC180 
(1,152 Wh) adds approximately 6 km. These are not "get home" numbers
for most scenarios — they are "get to a safe place to wait for a tow" numbers
or "get the last 2 km to the charger you misjudged" numbers.
 The Charging Rate Limitation
Most portable power stations deliver 120 V AC at 10–15 A (1,200–1,800 W
continuous). This is equivalent to a Level 1 EV charger — the slowest AC
charging standard. An EV's onboard charger will draw at the rate the power
station can supply, typically 8–12 A at 120 V (960–1,440 W).
This means a portable power station cannot deliver its full capacity to the EV
at a high rate; it delivers it slowly over 30–90 minutes depending on the
station's capacity. For a 768 Wh unit discharging at 1,000 W, the
transfer takes approximately 45 minutes. The EV is stationary during this
period — the "top-up while you wait" scenario, not "charge while driving."
Critically, the EV's onboard charger may refuse to engage if the power
station's voltage sags under load. Modified sine wave inverters (present in
some budget power stations) are particularly prone to this; the EV's charger
detects the non-sinusoidal waveform and refuses to charge as a protective
measure. Pure sine wave inverters — standard on all units recommended on this
site, as detailed in our inverter analysis 
— are compatible with all EV onboard chargers tested.
 Practical Use Cases
 Scenario Viable? Notes 
 EV ran out 2 km from charger — power station in trunk Yes A 500–800 Wh unit provides 3–5 km. Sufficient if the charger is truly that close. 
 EV at 5% SOC in a multi-day outage — power station for critical systems Yes Don't use the power station to charge the EV. Use it to power your refrigerator, CPAP, and communication equipment. The EV's battery (40–100 kWh) is a far larger energy reserve than any portable unit. 
 Pre-heating EV cabin before departure during outage Marginal Cabin heaters draw 3–7 kW. A portable power station cannot supply this. Use the EV's own battery for pre-heating — it's a rounding error on a 60 kWh pack. 
 Road trip emergency — no chargers for 50 km No A portable power station cannot provide 50 km of range. This requires a generator or a tow. 
 Keeping 12 V battery charged during long-term parking Yes A small power station or solar maintainer can keep the EV's 12 V accessory battery from draining, which prevents the "dead 12 V = bricked EV" failure mode that affects some models. 
 Vehicle-to-Load: The Inverse Use Case
Some EVs — including certain Hyundai, Kia, and Ford models — support
Vehicle-to-Load (V2L), which allows the EV's traction battery to power
external AC loads through an adapter. In this configuration, the EV's
40–100 kWh battery becomes the largest portable power station you own.
A single charge provides weeks of home backup for critical loads.
V2L turns the portable-power-station-for-EV question on its head: instead of
a 0.7 kWh power station charging a 60 kWh EV, a 60 kWh EV powers
your home during an outage. The power station becomes redundant for users with
V2L-capable EVs, except for portability (carrying power away from the vehicle)
or as a UPS buffer for electronics during the switchover.
If you own a V2L-capable EV, the optimal preparedness strategy is a
V2L adapter ($200–400, manufacturer-specific) rather than a standalone portable
power station. The cost per kWh of the EV's battery, already purchased, is
effectively zero for this use case.
 Recommendation
A portable power station as an EV emergency charger is a niche use case with
limited practical benefit — 3–6 km of range for a $400–800 investment.
The same money buys a more capable power station for home backup, or toward
a V2L adapter if your EV supports it. The power station earns its keep during
an outage by powering your home's critical loads; the EV, with its vastly
larger battery, handles transportation.
If you specifically want EV emergency top-up capability, the minimum viable
configuration is an
 EcoFlow River 2 Pro 
(768 Wh, pure sine wave, 800 W continuous) with the EV's Level 1
charging cable. Expect approximately 4 km of range per full discharge.
Treat it as insurance against the last-mile failure case, not as a range
extender.

Can a Portable Power Station Charge an EV? Emergency Guide 
 Skip to content 
 Can a portable power station charge an EV? Yes, in some setups it can add emergency range, but that is very different from using a normal home or public EV charger. The limiting factors are the power station’s battery capacity, AC output, outlet type, the EV charging equipment you use and the vehicle’s own charging requirements.
 The most useful way to think about this is emergency top-up . A high-capacity portable power station can potentially add enough energy to reach a safer location or nearby charger, but it should not be treated as a practical replacement for routine EV charging.
 For a verified current example, Anker explicitly supports EV charging from the SOLIX F3800 through its NEMA 14-50 outlet and EV mode. We use that exact product as the commercial reference instead of assuming that every large portable power station supports EV charging the same way.
 What Actually Has to Work?
 Four pieces have to line up before an EV can charge safely from a portable power station:
 The power station: it needs sufficient AC output and a manufacturer-supported outlet/configuration for the charging setup.
 The EVSE or charging cable: it must be compatible with the outlet and vehicle.
 The vehicle: it must accept the charging configuration being supplied.
 The connection method: use manufacturer-supported hardware and settings rather than improvised adapter chains.
 This is why “the station has enough watts” is not enough by itself.
 Affiliate disclosure: SunergyHub may earn a commission from qualifying purchases made through links on this page, at no additional cost to you. Recommendations are based on product fit and verified manufacturer information, not commission rate.
 Verified Example: Anker SOLIX F3800
 The Anker SOLIX F3800 is a useful reference because Anker explicitly documents EV charging on the current U.S. product page.
 Anker lists the F3800 with 3,840Wh of capacity, 6,000W continuous AC output , 120V/240V dual-voltage operation and a NEMA 14-50 outlet rated up to 6,000W .
 For EV charging, Anker instructs users to connect through the NEMA 14-50 port and double-press the 240V power switch to activate EV mode before recharging the vehicle.
 That manufacturer-documented EV mode is the reason we use the F3800 as the reference example. It does not mean every station with a 240V outlet should be assumed EV-compatible.
 Check Anker SOLIX F3800 Price 
 How Much EV Range Can a Portable Power Station Add?
 The answer depends on battery capacity, charging losses and the vehicle’s energy consumption. The correct way to estimate it is:
 Estimated added miles = station capacity (kWh) × assumed usable-to-EV efficiency ÷ vehicle consumption (kWh per mile) 
 SunergyHub example only: using the F3800’s 3.84kWh nameplate capacity, an illustrative 85% usable-to-EV efficiency assumption and an EV consuming 0.30kWh per mile:
 3.84 × 0.85 ÷ 0.30 ≈ 10.9 miles of estimated added range. 
 This is a calculation, not an Anker range claim and not a guarantee. A different EV, temperature, charging rate or conversion efficiency changes the result. The example is meant to show why even a large 3.84kWh portable station is primarily an emergency top-up tool compared with the much larger traction battery in an EV.
 Why Portable Power Stations Are Not a Normal EV-Charging Replacement
 Portable power stations are useful because they store energy you can move. EV traction batteries are much larger, so transferring a few kilowatt-hours from a portable station usually adds only a limited amount of range.
 That can still be valuable in an emergency. The goal may be to add enough range to leave a stranded location, reach a nearby charger or move the vehicle to a safer place. It is not efficient to use a portable power station as your routine way of refilling an EV.
 Can Smaller Portable Power Stations Charge an EV?
 Do not assume they can. A smaller unit may have enough energy to be interesting on paper but lack the outlet, voltage, manufacturer-supported charging mode or sustained output required by the EVSE.
 For that reason, this guide does not publish a generic list of “EV-compatible” power stations. We only use an exact manufacturer-documented example and recommend checking the station, EVSE and vehicle manuals for any other setup.
 What About Solar Charging the Power Station First?
 Solar can recharge a compatible portable power station, but that does not turn it into a fast EV charger. Solar input is limited by the station and the available sunlight, and the stored energy still has to be transferred from the station to the vehicle.
 If your goal is emergency resilience rather than daily EV charging, solar can still be useful because it gives the portable station another way to recover energy when the grid is unavailable.
 For broader high-capacity backup options, see our best solar generator for home backup and best 2000Wh portable power stations . For capacity planning, use what size solar generator do I need? For a broader product overview, see best portable solar generators .
 EV Emergency-Charging Checklist
 Confirm that the power-station manufacturer supports the intended EV charging method.
 Confirm the EVSE input and outlet requirements.
 Confirm the vehicle accepts the charging setup.
 Use the correct manufacturer-supported mode or setting.
 Estimate added range from stored kWh, losses and your EV’s actual consumption.
 Treat the setup as emergency range support, not normal charging infrastructure.
 FAQ
 Can a portable power station charge a Tesla?
 Potentially, but the exact charging equipment, outlet and vehicle requirements must all be compatible. Do not assume that every portable power station can charge every Tesla model. Use a manufacturer-supported setup and the charging equipment specified for your vehicle.
 How many miles can a power station add to an EV?
 It depends on the station’s stored energy, charging losses and the EV’s consumption. Our illustrative F3800 calculation using 3.84kWh, an 85% efficiency assumption and 0.30kWh per mile gives about 10.9 miles. That is an example calculation, not a manufacturer range claim.
 Can I use a portable power station instead of a home EV charger?
 No. A portable station can be useful for emergency top-up in a supported setup, but its battery capacity is far smaller than an EV traction battery. Routine home or public charging is the appropriate solution for normal EV use.
 Which portable power station is verified for EV charging?
 Anker explicitly documents EV charging on the SOLIX F3800 through its NEMA 14-50 outlet and EV mode. This guide does not generalize that compatibility to other models unless their manufacturers document it.
 Final Verdict
 A portable power station can charge an EV in the right manufacturer-supported setup, but its best role is emergency range addition. The Anker SOLIX F3800 is a verified example because Anker documents NEMA 14-50 EV charging and a dedicated EV mode.
 The key is to think in kilowatt-hours, not just watts. Even a powerful station can only transfer the energy stored in its battery, so emergency top-up is realistic; replacing normal EV charging is not.

Even if charging starts, the stored energy in a portable power station is small compared with the battery in a modern EV, so the extra range is usually modest.
 That is why this topic often sounds more promising in ads than it feels in real use. Charging the car and usefully charging the car are not always the same thing.

 Most shoppers look at the battery size first. That makes sense, but it is only half the picture. Whether a portable power station can help with EV charging depends on two separate limits:
 Power output determines whether the charger will run at all.
 Battery capacity determines how much range you may gain before the station is empty.
 A station may have enough stored energy to add a few miles, but still fail because the charger asks for more power than the inverter can provide.  When it actually makes sense
 A portable power station makes the most sense when the goal is limited backup charging, not routine charging. That distinction matters. Used in the right situation, it can still be genuinely useful.

Can A Portable Power Station Charge A Car Battery? 
 Cars 
 Can A Portable Power Station Charge A Car Battery?
 By   Joseph Chidi 
 June 17, 2025 10:00 am EST 
 Igor Kovalenko/Getty 
 Add SlashGear on Google:
 Preferred Source 
 Google Discover 
 We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. 
 Trying to get your car battery some juice while on a camping trip, or is your car just stranded with a dead battery? If you happen to have a portable power station (PPS) at hand, you could possibly charge your battery enough to start the engine. 
 Now, if by "battery" you meant an EV battery, now that's a different story. Most portable power stations don't have the voltage or capacity to handle a fully electric vehicle's battery. That said, if your PPS has a 120V AC outlet and can also deliver at least 1,200W continuously, you could use a standard  level 1 EV wall outlet charger to slowly (and inefficiently) get some power into your EV. That could be helpful if you just need a tiny bit of range to get to another location in an emergency.
 What we'll focus on here is charging the 12V battery found in gas-powered or hybrid vehicles, and some modern EVs , too. What kind of power station can do it? What specs matter? And how long will it take to get enough charge to turn the key?
 What power station specs do you need for a 12V car battery
 shine.graphics/Shutterstock 
 Assuming you've got a 12V car battery ready that's worth recharging , the first thing you'll need is a power station with a DC output — typically a cigarette lighter port that delivers more than 12.6V. That's because a healthy lead-acid 12V car battery at rest usually sits around 12.4V to 12.6V, and you need a higher voltage to push current into it.
 If your power station's DC output delivers less than that, it likely won't charge the battery effectively, especially if the battery is deeply discharged. While your power station's manual may label the output as "12V," many higher-end units actually regulate it at 13.2V to 13.6V, which is better suited for basic battery charging.
 For example, the 12V 30A DC output on the Bluetti AC200MAX is regulated at 13.5V, which means it can supply power until your battery reaches that same voltage. Once the battery approaches 13.5V, the charging current will slow down or stop because the voltage difference between the source and the battery gets too small to keep pushing energy in. if you're not sure what voltage your battery or power station is currently putting out, you can check using a digital multimeter.
 Next, you need to look at your portable power station's capacity in watt-hours. Car batteries would need between 400 to 800Wh (depending on the voltage and amp-hour combination) so you should have a power station with around 1,000Wh — accounting for inefficiencies and energy loss.
 How do you charge a car battery with a power station?
 Andrey Zhernovoy/Shutterstock 
 Once you've confirmed your power station meets the recommended specs, you'll need to get a DC-DC battery charger (like this 50A Renogy ), a DC power cable to plug the PPS to the battery charger, and of course battery cables to connect your car battery to the battery charger. These requirements might change depending on your battery, so make sure to look at the fine print. Now, you just leave it to charge, and it should take about six hours to fully charge a 12V 50A battery using a 12V 10A DC outlet on your PPS.
 On the other hand, you could just use the 120V AC outlet on most power stations. It works like a car battery wall-charger, converting the power station's AC to DC for battery charging. The reason we don't recommend this is that it's not as efficient, and you can expect to lose up to 20% of power due to converting DC to AC and then to DC again.

How to Charge an Electric Vehicle with a Power Station in an Emergency | VoltVanguard How to Charge an Electric Vehicle with a Power Station in an Emergency
 Updated May 2026
 Affiliate disclosure: This site contains affiliate links. We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you if you buy through them. We never accept payment for coverage and our picks are editorial. As electric vehicles become mainstream, EV owners face a unique emergency scenario: what happens when the power goes out and your car is sitting at 15% charge? Portable power stations offer a partial solution — not a fast one, but potentially enough to add critical range to reach a working charging station. This guide covers the fundamentals of EV charging from a power station, which units can actually do it, how much range you can realistically add, and the hard limitations that every EV owner needs to understand before relying on this strategy.
 How EV Charging from a Power Station Works
 Electric vehicles charge from AC power through their onboard charger, which converts AC to DC for the battery. In the US, Level 1 charging uses a standard 120V outlet (NEMA 5-15) at 12 amps, delivering approximately 1.4kW of power. Level 2 charging uses 240V at higher amperage, delivering 3-19kW. No portable power station can provide Level 2 charging — the voltage and amperage requirements are far too high. However, several large power stations support Level 1 charging at 120V and up to 12-15 amps. This means you can plug your EV's factory charging cable (the one that came with your car) into a compatible power station's AC outlet and add charge to your vehicle's battery. The process works exactly like plugging into a garage wall outlet — just slower and with far less total energy available.
 Power Station Requirements for EV Charging
 To charge an EV at Level 1, your power station must meet these minimum specs: (1) Continuous AC output of at least 1,500W. The EV's onboard charger will attempt to draw 1,400-1,500W (12A at 120V). If your power station can't sustain this, the EV will either charge at a reduced rate or the power station will shut down from overload. (2) Surge rating of at least 2,000W. EV chargers have a brief startup surge when the car negotiates the connection. (3) Capacity of at least 2,000Wh for meaningful range addition. At 1,400W draw with 85% inverter efficiency, you use approximately 1,650Wh per hour of charging. A 2,000Wh unit provides about 1 hour of actual charging after accounting for overhead. (4) Pure sine wave output. All quality power stations have this, but verify — EV onboard chargers are sensitive to power quality.
 How Much Range Can You Actually Add?
 This is where expectations must be realistic. Most EVs achieve 3-4 miles of range per kWh of energy stored. Level 1 charging delivers about 1.4kW to the vehicle, but accounting for charging losses (10-15%), the actual energy entering the battery is approximately 1.2kW per hour. Range added per hour: 1.2kWh x 3.5 miles/kWh = approximately 4.2 miles per hour of charging.
 With a 2,000Wh power station: - Usable AC energy: 2,000Wh x 0.85 = 1,700Wh - Charging losses: 1,700Wh x 0.85 = 1,445Wh delivered to EV battery - Range added: 1,445Wh x 3.5 miles/kWh / 1,000 = approximately 5 miles
 With a 3,000Wh unit (e.g., with expansion battery): - Range added: approximately 7.5 miles
 This is not a practical daily charging solution — it's an emergency bridge. A 2,000Wh power station can add roughly 5 miles of range, enough to get you to the nearest working charging station if you're close. It cannot replace regular home charging or serve as a substitute for a Level 2 installation.
 Compatible Power Stations for EV Charging
 Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 (2400W output, 2048Wh, $1,299) — The highest-output consumer power station, providing approximately 5 miles of emergency range. The 2400W continuous output handles EV Level 1 charging with headroom to spare: https://www.amazon.com/s?k=portable+power+station&tag=voltvanguard0626-20.
 Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 (2200W output, 2042Wh, $999) — Slightly lower output than the Anker C2000 Gen 2 but still sufficient for Level 1 EV charging. Adds approximately 5 miles of range: https://www.amazon.com/s?k=portable+power+station&tag=voltvanguard0626-20.
 Anker SOLIX C2000 Plus (2400W output, 4096Wh with expansion, $1,999) — With the optional expansion battery, this setup can add approximately 10 miles of range — the most practical consumer setup for EV emergency charging: https://www.amazon.com/s?k=portable+power+station&tag=voltvanguard0626-20.
 EGO POWER+ PST3040 (2000W output, up to 2.7kWh with 4x batteries, $499+ batteries) — The modular approach lets you hot-swap batteries for continuous charging. With a large battery collection, you can sustain charging for multiple hours by rotating charged batteries: https://www.amazon.com/s?k=portable+power+station&tag=voltvanguard0626-20.
 Practical Emergency Strategy for EV Owners
 If you own an EV and want a power station as emergency backup: (1) Buy the largest capacity you can afford and transport — 2,000Wh minimum, 3,000Wh+ preferred. (2) Reduce the EV's charging amperage if your power station can't handle full Level 1 load. Some EVs let you set the charging rate in the car's settings — reducing from 12A to 8A drops the load to 960W, which smaller power stations can sustain (though charging speed drops proportionally). (3) Charge during the day with solar supplementation. A 400W solar panel array can add 1,200-1,600Wh during good sun hours, extending your daily charge session. (4) Combine power station charging with other emergency strategies: AAA membership with EV towing, knowledge of nearby charging station locations, and keeping the car charged above 50% whenever possible during storm season. (5) Consider the power station's primary value as home backup for lights and refrigeration, with EV charging as a secondary emergency capability — not the primary reason to buy.
 Quick Tips
 A 2,000Wh power station adds only about 5 miles of EV range — use it as a last resort, not a charging strategy.
 Reduce your EV's charging amperage to 8A if your power station overloads at 12A.
 Charge during the day with solar panels to supplement the power station's capacity.
 Always keep your EV above 50% during storm season to minimize emergency charging needs.
 The power station's real value is home backup; EV charging is a bonus emergency feature.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can any power station charge an electric vehicle?
 No. Only power stations with 1,500W+ continuous AC output can handle Level 1 EV charging. The Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 at 2400W is the most capable consumer option: https://www.amazon.com/s?k=portable+power+station&tag=voltvanguard0626-20. Smaller units like the C300 (300W) or C800 (1200W) cannot sustain the 1,400W draw of an EV charger and will shut down from overload protection.
 How long does it take to charge an EV from a power station?
 A fully charged 2,000Wh power station provides approximately 1 hour of Level 1 charging, adding roughly 4-5 miles of range depending on your vehicle's efficiency. A 3,000Wh setup provides about 1.5 hours and 6-7 miles. This is not comparable to wall charging — it's an emergency bridge only.
 Can I use a power station to charge a Tesla?
 Yes. Tesla vehicles include a Mobile Connector with a NEMA 5-15 adapter that plugs into any standard 120V outlet. Plug this into your power station's AC outlet and the Tesla will charge at Level 1 speeds (approximately 3-4 miles per hour of charging). All Tesla models work with this method, though charging speed varies slightly by model.
 Does charging an EV from a power station damage the battery?
 No. The power from a quality LiFePO4 power station is clean pure sine wave — identical to grid power in terms of what your EV's onboard charger sees. The EV's charging system manages the actual battery charging and is unaffected by the source being a power station versus a wall outlet. The only difference is capacity — you'll run out of power station energy long before any damage could occur.
 Is there a better emergency charging solution than a power station?
 For serious EV emergency preparedness, a gas generator provides far more charging capacity. A 3,000W generator can sustain Level 1 charging indefinitely with fuel and adds Level 2 capability (240V) for much faster charging. However, generators require fuel storage, produce exhaust, and can't be used indoors. Many EV owners use both — a power station for silent indoor home backup and a generator for EV charging and major appliances.
